title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 74 (Compensation for breach where penalty is stipulated)

content.overview: Section 74 applies where a contract names a sum payable on breach or contains another stipulation by way of penalty. The party complaining of breach may receive reasonable compensation, whether or not actual loss or damage is proved, but the award cannot exceed the named sum or stipulated penalty. The section includes an explanation about increased interest after default, an exception for specified public-duty bonds and related instruments, and statutory illustrations. The topic is in review pending current-amendment reconciliation and any further source/release gates.

sections.heading: Statutory trigger and cap
sections.body: Identify a broken contract and either (a) a sum named as payable on breach or (b) another contractual stipulation by way of penalty. The statutory remedy is reasonable compensation, capped at the sum named or penalty stipulated; the clause itself does not automatically dictate the amount awarded.

sections.heading: Actual loss and reasonable compensation
sections.body: The statutory wording says reasonable compensation may be awarded whether or not actual loss or damage is proved. This does not authorise a windfall or compensation where no legal injury has resulted. Assess reasonableness on the facts and the principles applicable to the claim.

sections.heading: Forfeiture and deposits
sections.body: Section 74 can apply to a contractual penalty stipulation involving forfeiture of money or property already delivered. Do not assume that every payment labelled earnest money, deposit, or advance has the same legal character; examine the contract, purpose of payment, breach, evidence and applicable authority.

sections.heading: Increased interest after default
sections.body: The statutory Explanation states that a stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty. Compare the contractual rates and operation of the clause; the label used by the parties is not by itself decisive.

sections.heading: Statutory exception
sections.body: The section contains an exception for a bail-bond, recognizance or similar instrument, and specified bonds given under law or government order for performance of a public duty or act in which the public are interested. The accompanying Explanation says a contract with Government does not necessarily, by itself, mean a public duty or an act in which the public are interested. Check that the facts fit the exception before relying on it.

sections.heading: Statutory illustrations
sections.body: The illustrations distinguish a sum stipulated on breach, a restraint-related penalty, recognizance forfeiture, increased default interest, an increased quantity obligation, and acceleration of a loan balance. Apply the exact illustration and its conditions; do not generalise a result to materially different contract terms.

sections.heading: Evidence and application
sections.body: Preserve the signed contract and relevant clause, proof of breach, payment/deposit records, evidence of loss or legal injury, calculation of the claimed amount, and facts bearing on reasonableness. State the contractual ceiling separately from the amount claimed and the amount that may reasonably be awarded.

examples.title: Named sum on breach
examples.body: A contract says ₹50,000 is payable on breach. The court assesses reasonable compensation under Section 74 and cannot exceed ₹50,000; the contractual number is a ceiling, not automatic proof that the whole amount is reasonable.

examples.title: Forfeiture clause
examples.body: A seller seeks to forfeit money already paid under a contract after the other party's breach. Analyse whether the clause is a stipulation by way of penalty, the legal character of the payment, the breach and the reasonable compensation supported by the circumstances.

examples.title: Increased interest on default
examples.body: A loan agreement stipulates a sharp increase in interest only after default. Section 74's Explanation specifically identifies increased interest from default as a possible penalty stipulation; assess the actual clause rather than assuming every default-rate clause is invalid.

examples.title: Public-duty bond
examples.body: A party invokes the statutory exception for a bond. Establish that the instrument and public-duty conditions fall within the exception; a contract with Government alone does not necessarily establish the exception.

hypotheticals.question: A contract names ₹1,00,000 as payable on breach, but the claimant provides little evidence of loss. Is ₹1,00,000 automatically recoverable?
hypotheticals.analysis: No automatic conclusion follows from the figure alone. Section 74 permits reasonable compensation within the stated ceiling, whether or not actual loss is proved, but it does not authorise a windfall where no legal injury resulted. Assess the clause and circumstances.

hypotheticals.question: A party seeks to forfeit an advance after the other party breaches the contract. What should be analysed?
hypotheticals.analysis: Read the clause and payment records; determine the purpose and character of the amount, whether forfeiture is a penalty stipulation, what breach occurred, and what reasonable compensation is justified. The cap is the amount named or penalty stipulated.

hypotheticals.question: A contract with a government department includes a bond penalty. Does the statutory exception necessarily apply?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 74's Explanation says a contract with Government does not necessarily mean the contractor undertook a public duty or an act in which the public are interested. Establish the statutory exception's actual conditions.

illustrations: Section 74 illustration (a): a sum is named for failure to pay a smaller sum on a given day; compensation may be awarded only up to the named ceiling and as the court considers reasonable.
Section 74 illustration (d): a sharp increase in interest from default is described as a stipulation by way of penalty.
Section 74 illustration (f): acceleration of the whole loan after an instalment default is illustrated as not being a penalty on those stated facts; the specific contractual structure matters.
Section 74 includes a specific exception for qualifying bail-bonds, recognizances and certain public-duty instruments.

learningObjectives: Identify the contractual triggers for Section 74.
Explain the reasonable-compensation rule and statutory ceiling.
Apply the statutory text to penalty, forfeiture, increased-interest and public-duty-bond issues.
Use verified case authority cautiously and distinguish the rule from Sections 73 and 75.
enhancement.definition: Section 74 governs reasonable compensation where a contract names a sum payable on breach or contains another stipulation by way of penalty, subject to the statutory ceiling and exception.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A party complaining of breach may receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named or penalty stipulated, whether or not actual loss is proved; the provision does not authorise a windfall where no legal injury has resulted.

essentialIngredients: Identify the named sum or other penalty stipulation
Assess reasonable compensation in the circumstances
Check whether the statutory exception applies
For forfeiture or increased-interest clauses, analyse the actual terms and facts
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 74 applies when a contract is broken and either a sum is named as payable on breach or another stipulation by way of penalty is included. The remedy is reasonable compensation up to the contractual ceiling, whether or not actual loss is proved. The ceiling is not an automatic entitlement to the whole amount. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das, the Supreme Court explained that the provision requires reasonable compensation and does not justify an award where no legal injury resulted; it also considered forfeiture under a penalty stipulation. Section 74's text separately addresses increased interest after default and creates an exception for specified public-duty bonds and similar instruments. A government contract alone does not necessarily establish that exception. Apply the actual contractual terms and evidence.
examples: Named sum on breach: compensation is assessed as reasonable and cannot exceed the named ceiling.
Forfeiture: examine the payment's character and penalty clause rather than assuming every deposit is forfeitable.
Increased interest: consider the statutory Explanation and the actual rate change after default.
Public-duty bond: prove the specific conditions of the statutory exception.
distinctions: Section 73 generally addresses compensation for loss caused by breach; Section 74 addresses a named sum or other penalty stipulation and imposes a ceiling.
Section 75 addresses compensation for damage sustained through rightful rescission after non-fulfilment.
The contractual ceiling is not itself proof that the entire amount is reasonable compensation.
The public-duty-bond exception is not triggered merely because the contract is with Government.
caseLaw: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das, AIR 1963 SC 1405; 1964 SCR (1) 515 — official Supreme Court judgment: https://api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/3634.pdf
problemApplication: Quote the relevant contractual stipulation and identify the breach.
Determine whether the clause names a sum or is otherwise by way of penalty.
Assess the facts bearing on reasonable compensation and any legal injury.
Analyse forfeiture, increased interest or the public-duty exception if relevant.
Conclude without treating the named amount as automatically payable.

keyTakeaways: Section 74 grants reasonable compensation, not automatic enforcement of the full stipulated amount.
The named sum or penalty is a ceiling.
Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das is an official Supreme Court authority on reasonable compensation and penalty forfeiture.
A government contract alone does not establish the public-duty exception.

caseLaw: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das, AIR 1963 SC 1405; 1964 SCR (1) 515 (Supreme Court judgment opened at https://api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/3634.pdf). The Court treated Section 74 as requiring reasonable compensation subject to the stipulated ceiling, and addressed penalty clauses and forfeiture; the judgment also states that Section 74 does not justify compensation where no legal injury resulted.
